summary: This memo is a glossary of networking terms specific to the Internet, written to help people new to the field. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1983.

plainLanguage.summary: A glossary is a small dictionary, and this one explains the words people use about the Internet, from technical terms like datagram to jokes like the typed smiley face. It came out in January 1993 for readers new to networking, and it has since been replaced by RFC 1983.

questions: what do internet networking terms mean
subtitle: A 1993 dictionary of Internet terms, written for people who had just arrived.

tldr.problem: People meeting the Internet in the early 1990s ran into a wall of acronyms and jargon, and the existing networking glossaries covered the whole field rather than the Internet's own vocabulary.
tldr.mechanism: The User Glossary Working Group collected short definitions of Internet-specific terms into one alphabetical glossary, with cross-references between entries, credits for where definitions came from, and a References list for further reading.
tldr.outcome: It gave newcomers a single place to look up terms from ARPANET to the smiley face. It is an Informational RFC and has been obsoleted by RFC 1983, an expanded version.

sections.title: What This Glossary Is
sections.content:
RFC 1392 is the Internet Users' Glossary, published as FYI 18 in January 1993 and edited by Gary Malkin and Tracy LaQuey Parker. The abstract explains its place among the many networking glossaries already in existence: this one concentrates on terms specific to the Internet, with entries for basic terms and acronyms added because other entries refer to them.

The document is the work of the User Glossary Working Group in the User Services Area of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). The acknowledgements give special thanks to Jon Postel for his definition of datagram, which the glossary uses.

Its audience is the person meeting the network for the first time. Entries cover the protocols, devices, organisations and habits of the Internet as they stood at the start of 1993.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a dictionary of Internet words for people new to the network, put together by an IETF working group and published in January 1993.

sections.title: How the Entries Work
sections.content:
Entries run alphabetically, with a short section before A for terms starting with a digit or symbol. Each entry gives a definition in a few lines and often ends with See also, listing related entries so the reader can travel through the vocabulary. Some entries are pure signposts: ACK says See: Acknowledgment, and 822 says See: RFC 822.

Many definitions carry a bracketed source, either an RFC or one of the works in the References list, so a reader can tell where the wording came from. The datagram entry, credited to J. Postel, defines it as a self-contained, independent entity of data carrying enough information to be routed from source to destination without reliance on earlier exchanges. The Address Resolution Protocol entry names RFC 826 and warns that ARP works only on physical networks that support broadcast packets.

Not every entry is technical. The symbol entry :-) explains that the typed smiley face conveys mood in the flat medium of computers, that there are hundreds of such symbols, and that smiles are also used to denote sarcasm; the reader having trouble seeing it is told to tilt their head 90 degrees to the left. The entry for Cyberspace credits the term to William Gibson's novel Neuromancer. The cracker entry contrasts crackers, who break into systems without authorization and are often malicious, with hackers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry is a short definition, usually with pointers to related entries and a note of where the wording came from. Some entries are plain signposts, and some cover culture as well as technology, such as the typed smiley face and the word cyberspace.

sections.title: A Picture of the Internet in Early 1993
sections.content:
Because the glossary defines the terms of its moment, it doubles as a snapshot. ARPANET, the Advanced Research Projects Agency Network, is described as a pioneering long-haul network funded by ARPA, now DARPA, that served as the basis for early networking research and as a central backbone during the Internet's development; it consisted of packet-switching computers joined by leased lines.

The entry for CREN, the Corporation for Research and Educational Networking, records that it was formed in October 1989 when Bitnet and CSNET were combined under one administrative authority, that CSNET is no longer operational, and that CREN still runs Bitnet. The glossary also carries entries for then-current technology such as Asynchronous Transfer Mode, described as carrying data in fixed-size packets called cells, and for Kerberos, the security system of MIT's Project Athena, and points to the World Wide Web.

The References list shows what a well-read newcomer of the time was expected to consult: F.Y.I. documents, the RFC series, the Jargon File, and books such as Comer's Internetworking with TCP/IP, Tanenbaum's Computer Networks and Kehoe's Zen and the Art of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Since it defines the words of its time, the glossary also shows what the Internet looked like in 1993: which networks and organisations still existed, which had faded, and which books a newcomer was expected to read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is one paragraph. It says that security is not explicitly discussed in the document, but that some of its entries are security related, and it points the reader to them: Access Control List, authentication, Computer Emergency Response Team, cracker, Data Encryption Key, Data Encryption Standard, encryption, Kerberos, Privacy Enhanced Mail, Trojan Horse, virus and worm.
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary does not teach security, but it defines the security words a reader will meet, and the security section lists those entries.

data.code:
datagram
  A self-contained, independent entity of data carrying sufficient
  information to be routed from the source to the destination
  computer without reliance on earlier exchanges between this source
  and destination computer and the transporting network.  See also:
  frame, packet.
  [Source: J. Postel]

ACK
  See: Acknowledgment
